abstract: Mitochondrial dynamics are essential for cellular health and fertility, yet how mitochondrial ultrastructure adapts during gametogenesis and acute environmental stress remains poorly understood. Here, using high-pressure freezing electron microscopy and automated quantitative morphometry (EMito-Metrix), we mapped mitochondrial ultrastructure across the Caenorhabditis elegans germline and somatic tissues. We reveal that mitochondria undergo progressive structural maturation during germ cell differentiation, transitioning from small, round profiles to elongated networks with aligned cristae. Following short oxidative stress, differentiating germ cells and early embryos, unlike somatic or sperm cells, undergo a remarkable morphological remodeling to form protective, fusion-dependent donut-shaped and vacuolated spheroid mitochondria. Genetic disruption of the mitochondrial fusion factor fzo-1 blocks this pathway and results in a collapse of stress-induced brood size. These results demonstrate that atypical mitochondrial morphotypes are not passive markers of damage, but an active, FZO-1-dependent defense strategy shielding female gametes. This work highlights the C. elegans gonad as a versatile model to explore mitochondrial plasticity, reproductive aging, and environmental toxicology.
